full_text: D 018 01 EXECUTIVE ORDER Creation of the Office of Preparedness and Security Under the Department of Public Safety Pursuant to the authority vested in the Office of the Governor of the State of Colorado, I, Bill Owens, Governor of the State of Colorado, hereby issue this Executive Order transferring certain personnel to the Department of Public Safety and requesting coordination of certain executive departments in order to create the Office of Preparedness and Security. 1. Background and Purpose. The events of September 11, 2001 have highlighted the need within Colorado to coordinate state government responsiveness to public safety threats. Over the past two months, members of my cabinet have worked to identify the organizational and operational needs of state agencies in light of the new challenges facing public safety officials. State government must prepare for and respond to a range of new terrorism threats to public safety. In an effort to create and maintain a state government that is able to respond to the changing needs of its citizens, the general assembly has extended to the executive directors of the principal departments specific statutory authority in Colorado Revised Statute §24-1-107 to establish, combine or abolish divisions, sections and units of the agencies and to allocate and reallocate powers, duties and functions to divisions, sections and units under the principal department with the approval of the Governor as organizational needs change. Several executive directors have conducted a review of their departments and have reported to me that changes would be beneficial to enable their departments to better prepare for and respond to Colorado’s public safety needs. As envisioned by the Colorado Disaster Emergency Act of 1992, threats to the public safety of this magnitude confer upon the Governor unique powers and responsibilities. As Governor, I am responsible for meeting the dangers to the state and people presented by disasters. The Act defines disasters as the occurrence or imminent threat of widespread or severe damage injury or loss of life or property resulting from any natural cause or cause of human origin. Section 24-32-2104(7)(c) of the Act enables the Governor to transfer the direction, personnel, or functions of state departments and agencies or units thereof for the purpose of performing or facilitating emergency services. Therefore, under the authority given to me by the general assembly, I am creating the Office of Preparedness and Security within the Colorado Department of Public Safety. Through this executive order, I am also creating within the Office of Preparedness and Security the Office of Anti-Terrorism Planning and Training. 2. Mission. I hereby find that a state of disaster emergency has existed since September 11, 2001 and that this threat continues. Additionally, I find that the nature of the threat requires prudent measures such as reorganization or consolidation of certain functions of state government to allow for the greatest preparedness for and response to emerging threats against Colorado’s citizens and property. Pursuant to C.R.S. § 24-1-107, I approve the Department of Public Safety’s request for reorganization in order to establish the Office of Preparedness and Security and within this office the Office of Anti-Terrorism Planning and Training. Pursuant to C.R.S. § 24-32-2104(7)(c), I hereby transfer certain personnel and their functions to the Department of Public Safety for the creation of the Division of Anti- Terrorism Planning and Training located within the Office of Preparedness and Security. At the direction of the Executive Directors and with the approval of the Governor, I hereby transfer certain personnel and their functions in the Office of Emergency Management from the Department of Local Affairs to the Department of Public Safety. Under this same authority and process, I hereby transfer certain personnel and their functions from the Colorado Department of Health and Environment to the Department of Public Safety. I direct all executive departments and agencies of State Government to coordinate their public safety efforts as necessary with the Office of Preparedness and Security. 3. Duration. This Executive Order shall remain in force until modified or terminated by further executive order of the Governor. GIVEN under my hand and the Executive Seal of the State of Colorado, this 7th day of November, 2001. Bill Owens Governor

full_text: D 020 01 E X E C U T I V E O R D E R TRANSFERRING BUILD A GENERATION TO THE DEPARTMENT OF PUBLIC HEALTH AND ENVIRONMENT Pursuant to the authority vested in the Office of the Governor of the State of Colorado, I, Bill Owens, Governor of the State of Colorado, hereby issue this Executive Order transferring the Build A Generation program from the Colorado Department of Public Safety to the Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment. 1. Background and Purpose. Build A Generation is a prevention initiative for Colorado’s communities, designed to strengthen support systems for children. The Build A Generation process provides a framework for: • training of community key leaders; • identifying and prioritizing risk factors; • assessing how current resources are being used; • identifying community resource gaps; and • developing a comprehensive strategic prevention plan. Build A Generation is focused on supporting our children in developing and leading lives that are safe, productive, healthy and crime-free. This requires a willingness to change as well as a lasting commitment from local communities. Sustaining long-term change in a community requires, among other things, a coordinated effort to participate in and influence local public policy decision-making; collaboration among a number of different institutions, agencies, and organizations; and implementation of effective prevention programs and strategies. The philosophy of Build A Generation is consistent with programs in the newly formed Division of Prevention and Intervention Services for Children and Youth in the Department of Public Health and Environment. The Colorado General Assembly, in the 2000 legislative session, passed House Bill 1342 creating a single division in the Department of Public Health and Environment to operate and oversee the provision of state and federally-funded prevention and intervention programs. Through this legislation, the General Assembly sought to eliminate the dispersion and overlap among prevention and intervention programs, to ensure collaboration among programs operated by or funded through several state departments, and to make available a continuum of services for children and youth. 2. Mission. Since 1992, Build A Generation has been operated by the Division of Criminal Justice in the Department of Public Safety. I hereby order the transfer of Build A Generation from the Department of Public Safety to the Department of Public Health and Environment. 3. Duration. This Executive Order shall remain in force until modified or terminated by further Executive Order of the Governor. GIVEN under my hand and the Executive Seal of the State of Colorado, this 23rd day of December, 2001. Bill Owens Governor

full_text: D 004 02 EXECUTIVE ORDER Concerning a General Hiring Freeze in State Government Pursuant to the authority vested in the Office of the Governor of the State of Colorado and in particular Colorado Revised Statute § 24-2-102(4), I, Bill Owens, Governor of the State of Colorado, hereby issue this Executive Order implementing a hiring freeze applicable to state government. 1. Background and Purpose. In the past year, the national and Colorado economies have experienced significant slowdown. The events of September 11, 2001, compounded the economic slowdown in Colorado by further impacting our travel and tourism industry. Moreover, these economic conditions have caused the State to lose a considerable number of high wage telecommunications and advanced technology positions. As a result, there has been a decline in revenues to the State. In addition, constitutional requirements for state expenditures, such as Amendment 23, have limited the flexibility of the State to make budgetary corrections in response to economic recessions. To date, efforts to reduce general fund expenditures are not sufficient to satisfy the total reductions necessary to comply with the requirement of a balanced budget in Article X, Section 16 of the Colorado Constitution. As Governor, I am responsible for restricting the expenditure of state funds if it appears that a revenue shortfall may occur. Colorado Revised Statute § 24-2-102(4) provides: “If, during any fiscal period, there are not sufficient revenues available for expenditure during such period to carry on the functions of the state government and to support its agencies and institutions and such fact is made to appear to the governor, in the exercise of his discretion, by executive order, he may suspend or discontinue, in whole or in part, the functions or services of any department, board, bureau, or agency of the state government…” 2. Mission. I find that the threat of a revenue shortfall currently exists making it necessary to take the cost saving measure of suspending certain functions of state government. Pursuant to C.R.S. § 24-2-102(4), I order a hiring freeze applicable to state government. This hiring freeze is effective immediately. To protect the public health, safety and welfare of the citizens of the State and in order to avoid significant disruptions to critical state services, a process is provided in this Executive Order to allow certain exemptions to the hiring freeze. The Governor’s Office of State Planning and Budgeting, in conjunction with the Department of Personnel and Administration, shall provide general criteria to determine which vacant positions may be exempted from the hiring freeze. Each executive director of a statutorily created department shall review any requests for an exemption and may recommend exemptions they deem necessary to the Governor’s Office of State Planning and Budgeting. In higher education, the Director of the Colorado Commission on Higher Education shall review requests for exemptions from the head of each governing board and the Director may recommend exemptions he deems necessary to the Governor’s Office of State Planning and Budgeting. The Director of the Office of State Planning and Budgeting will then recommend any exemptions she approves to the Governor’s Chief of Staff. The Governor’s Chief of Staff shall determine whether a request shall be granted. 3. Elective Officers. I request that Elective Officers and the Judicial branch of the State of Colorado consider adopting a parallel hiring freeze to accommodate the cost saving objective of this Executive Order. 4. Duration. This Executive Order shall remain in force until June 1, 2002 unless modified or terminated by further executive order of the Governor. Pursuant to § 24-2-102(4), the Governor may extend this order by finding that a deficiency of revenues persists. GIVEN under my hand and the Executive Seal of the State of Colorado, this 28th day of February, 2002. Bill Owens Governor

full_text: D 007 02 EXECUTIVE ORDER Proclamation Pursuant to the Colorado Disaster Emergency Act Pursuant to the authority vested in the Office of the Governor of the State of Colorado, I, Bill Owens, Governor of the State of Colorado, hereby issue this Proclamation identifying the San Miguel County mudslides as qualifying under state law for state disaster emergency designation. 1. Background and Need On August 8, 2001, the Colorado Department of Transportation (“CDOT”) and several other agencies of Colorado State government responded to multiple mudslides in San Miguel County. Up to six feet of mud and other debris accumulated on State Highway 145 between the towns of Placerville and Telluride, Colorado trapping several vehicles and causing severe damage to the road system. The mudslides were a result of torrential rains over a two-hour period that produced flooding and runoff conditions. Repairs were required immediately to respond to the emergency conditions presented by the slides and to prevent further degradation of public safety and losses of public and private property due to the runoff conditions. CDOT immediately began repairs to the damaged roadway surfaces, drainage structures and began work to reinforce surrounding embankments, utilizing its contingency reserve funds. Local officials of the San Miguel Sheriff’s office declared that the mudslide and runoff conditions qualified as a disaster emergency. The devastation included the complete blockage of over 70 drainage structures; the headwalls or inlets of some highway structures were plugged or crushed. The roadway was completely filled with debris in sections. On the downhill side of the road, four remaining rock walls or crib walls were completely destroyed. The repair work needed to protect the public safety was provided by existing budget available through the Colorado Department of Transportation. 2. Proclamation For the purposes of this Proclamation and pursuant to the power and authority vested in the Office of the Governor by Colorado Revised Statute §24-32-2104, I declare that the San Miguel County mudslide of August 8, 2001, constituted a disaster for purposes of the Colorado Disaster Emergency Act, § 24-32-2103, C.R.S. Under the Act, disaster means “the occurrence or imminent threat of widespread or severe damage, injury, loss of life or property resulting from any natural cause or cause of human origin, including but not limited to fire, flood, earthquake, wind, storm, wave action, hazardous substance incident, oil spill or other water contamination requiring emergency action to avert danger or damage, volcanic activity, epidemic, air pollution, blight, drought infestation, explosion, civil disturbance, or hostile military or paramilitary action.” 3. Duration This Executive Order shall expire thirty (30) days from the date of its execution unless extended by Executive Order. GIVEN under my hand and the Executive Seal of the State of Colorado this 26th day of March, 2002. Bill Owens Governor

full_text: D 009 02 EXECUTIVE ORDER Declaring a Disaster Emergency Due to the Occurrence of Wildfires and the Imminent Threat of Additional Wildfire Activity Due to Drought Conditions Pursuant to the authority vested in the Office of the Governor of the State of Colorado and, in particular, Colorado Revised Statute § 24-32-2104, I, Bill Owens, Governor of the State of Colorado, hereby issue this Executive Order making certain funds available from the Emergency Management Fund for wildfire suppression and mitigation activities. 1. Background and Purpose. Due to drought conditions, Colorado’s 2002 fire season is approximately 6-7 weeks ahead of schedule. The western and southeastern parts of Colorado are facing severe drought conditions and the remainder of the state is facing moderate drought conditions. The Colorado Division of Forestry reports that 10-Hour Fuels (grasses, small woody twigs, and other brush) are currently at 1-4% of normal moisture and 1000 Hour Fuels (wood materials 3 inches and larger) are at 6-10% of normal moisture. Most significantly, 283 wildfires have already burned 7664 acres in the State of Colorado during the very early part of the 2002 fire season. These figures indicate that the potential for an active 2002 fire season is high. Enhanced suppression and mitigation activities are immediately necessary to respond to that risk. As envisioned by the Colorado Disaster Emergency Act of 1992, threats to the public safety of this magnitude confer upon the Governor unique powers and responsibilities. As Governor, I am responsible for meeting the dangers to the state and people presented by disasters. The Act defines disasters as the occurrence or imminent threat of widespread or severe damage, injury, or loss of life or property resulting from any natural cause or cause of human origin, including but not limited to fire. C.R.S. § 24-32-2103 (1.5). Because resources are immediately necessary to increase the level of fire suppression capability due to actual burning conditions and the imminent threat of additional fires, I issue this Executive Order making certain Emergency Management Funds immediately available for wildfire suppression and mitigation activities. 2. Mission. I hereby find that a state of disaster emergency exists due to the occurrence of wildfires. Additionally, I find that there is an imminent threat of additional wildfire activity due to drought conditions. Pursuant to C.R.S. § 24-32-2106, I order $450,000 in disaster emergency funds be made immediately available for wildfire suppression and mitigation activities. 3. Duration. This Executive Order shall expire thirty (30) days from its date of signature unless extended by Executive Order. GIVEN under my hand and the Executive Seal of the State of Colorado, this 23rd day of April, 2002. Bill Owens Governor

full_text: D 012 02 E X E C U T I V E O R D E R Open Burning and Fireworks Ban on State Lands Pursuant to the authority vested in the Office of the Governor of the State of Colorado, and in particular Article IV, Section 5 of the Colorado Constitution and Section 23-30-308 of the Colorado Revised Statutes, I, Bill Owens, Governor of the State of Colorado, hereby issue this Executive Order directing state agencies to prohibit open fires, including the use of fireworks, on all state lands. 1. Background and Need. There is no longer a need to speculate as to the level of fire danger within the State of Colorado. The state continues to experience severe drought conditions and we are in the midst of an extremely active wildfire season. To date, 510 fires have burned 42,083 acres during the very early part of the 2002 fire season. Given the present conditions of extreme fire danger, it is necessary to temporarily restrict human activities that have the potential of igniting a wildfire on our state lands. In response, this Executive Order bans open burning, including the use of fireworks, on all state lands. 2. Mission and Scope. A. I hereby order each state agency to ban open burning on lands under each agency’s jurisdiction or control. B. For purposes of this order, “open burning” is defined as any outdoor fire, including but not limited to campfires, warming fires, charcoal grill fires, fireworks and any other activity that poses a significant risk of starting a fire on state lands. C. For purposes of this order, “open burning” does not include: i. fires contained within liquid fueled or gas-fueled stoves; ii. fireplaces within buildings; and iii. permanent fire structures on developed or improved picnic grounds or campsites; and iv. prescribed or controlled burning for agricultural or irrigation purposes if approved in writing by the director of the administering agency overseeing the state land at issue. 3. Duration. This Executive Order shall remain in force until modified or terminated by further executive order of the Governor. GIVEN under my hand and the Executive Seal of the State of Colorado, this 4th day of June, 2002. Bill Owens Governor

full_text: D 013 02 EXECUTIVE ORDER AMENDMENT Concerning Commercial Fireworks Displays on State Lands and Amending Executive Order D 012 02 Pursuant to the authority vested in the Office of the Governor of the State of Colorado, and in particular Article IV, Section 5 of the Colorado Constitution and Section 23-30-308 of the Colorado Revised Statutes, I, Bill Owens, Governor of the State of Colorado, hereby issue this Executive Order amending D 012 02 by finding that commercial fireworks displays may be permitted on state lands upon written approval. 1. Background and Need. On June 4, 2002, I issued Executive Order D 012 02 directing state agencies to prohibit open burning on all state lands. This order included the prohibition of fireworks on state lands. The fire danger in our state is extremely high and I have determined that fireworks pose an unnecessary risk to our state lands. I have also encouraged the people of Colorado to attend commercial fireworks displays as an alternative to setting off their own fireworks. Commercial fireworks displays are performed by professionals with the cooperation of fire officials to ensure that the risk of igniting a fire is minimal. For this reason, I am permitting commercial fireworks displays on state lands if certain conditions are met. 2. Mission and Scope. For purposes of this Executive Order, “open burning” does not include commercial fireworks displays on state lands if the Executive Director managing the state land provides written approval in advance of the display. Before granting requests for commercial fireworks displays on state lands, the Executive Director must determine that appropriate measures have been taken to minimize the risk of the display causing a fire. This determination may include assurances from the local fire department that the display does not pose a significant fire risk and that the local fire department will be present at the fireworks display. To clarify, the Director of Natural Resources shall approve all requests for displays on lands controlled by the Division of Natural Resources and the Director of the Commission for Higher Education shall approve all requests for displays on lands occupied by state colleges or universities. 3. Duration. This Executive Order shall remain in force until modified or terminated by further executive order of the Governor. GIVEN under my hand and the Executive Seal of the State of Colorado, this 4th day of June, 2002. Bill Owens Governor

full_text: D 014 02 E X E C U T I V E O R D E R Declaring a Statewide Disaster Emergency Due to Wildfires and Ordering to State Active Duty Certain Elements of the Colorado National Guard Pursuant to the authority vested in the Office of the Governor of the State of Colorado, and in particular Article IV, Section 5 of the Colorado Constitution, and Sections 24-32-2100 et seq., and 23-30-308 of the Colorado Revised Statutes, I, Bill Owens, Governor of the State of Colorado, hereby issue this Executive Order declaring a state of disaster emergency and ordering to state active duty certain elements of the Colorado National Guard. 1. Background & Need. Colorado is experiencing the most dangerous wildfire season in the history of our state. Extraordinary measures are necessary to protect the public health, ensure public safety and render relief for those most severely impacted. I hereby declare a statewide disaster emergency due to wildfires and order to state active duty certain elements of the Colorado National Guard. Since April 23, 2002, over 250,000 acres have burned throughout the state. The frequency and number of wildfires since this date has stretched the state’s fire suppression personell dangerously thin and, for that reason, each of these wildfires has posed an imminent threat to life and property. Accordingly, I am declaring that wildfires occurring since April 23, 2002 constitute a disaster for purposes of § 24-32-2103, C.R.S. We must remain mindful that, technically speaking, the fire season has yet begun. Meanwhile the continuing drought along with unseasonably high temperatures is increasing the risk and danger of future wildfires throughout the state. For this reason, I am declaring a statewide disaster emergency due to the imminent threat of future wildfires. 2. Mission and Scope. A. Wildfires occurring after April 23, 2002 constitute a disaster for purposes of § 24-32-2103, C.R.S.; B. The threat of future wildfires constitutes a statewide disaster for purposes of § 24-32-2103, C.R.S.; C. In accordance with this disaster emergency, I hereby order the following: i) The transfer of funds into the Disaster Emergency Fund as ordered in the “Funding Directive” section and the expenditure of funds from the Disaster Emergency Fund. ii) The state activation of certain elements of the Colorado National Guard as may be determined from time to time by the Colorado Office of Emergency Management; iii) The authorization of all state departments and agencies to take whatever actions are required and requested by the Colorado Office of Emergency Management, within the Colorado State Emergency Operations Plan, to meet the emergency needs; iv) All previous and future verbal orders, until memorialized in a written order amending this Executive Order, which I may make in reference to this state disaster emergency shall have the full force and effect as if they were contained within this Executive Order. 3. Funding Directive It is the policy of the state that funds shall always be available to meet disaster emergencies. C.R.S. § 24-32-2106(1). I hereby find that the demands placed upon regularly appropriated funds and the disaster emergency fund are unreasonably great. Pursuant to C.R.S. § 24-32-2106(4), I hereby order the transfer of $10 million from the TABOR Emergency Reserve into the Disaster Emergency Fund. The Director of the Office of State Planning and Budgeting shall determine which particular TABOR Emergency Reserve accounts shall be deducted. 4. Duration. This Executive Order shall expire thirty (30) days from the date of its execution unless extended by Executive Order. GIVEN under my hand and the Executive Seal of the State of Colorado this 10th day of June, 2002. Bill Owens Governor

full_text: D 018 02 EXECUTIVE ORDER Directing Agencies of State Government to Assist in Meeting the Constitutional Requirements of a Balanced Budget Pursuant to the authority vested in the Office of the Governor of the State of Colorado and in particular Colorado Revised Statute § 24-2-102(4), I, Bill Owens, Governor of the State of Colorado, hereby issue this Executive Order directing agencies of state government to assist in meeting the constitutional requirements of a balanced budget, including the suspension of certain provider rates. 1. Background and Purpose. Similar to most states throughout the country, the State of Colorado is facing a substantial revenue shortfall. In fiscal year 2001-02, most General Fund expenditures were preserved through $1.2 billion of one-time revenues. Because these were one-time revenue sources, they maintained a revenue base in FY 2002-01 that was not sustainable in the future. Nonetheless, the fiscal year 2002-03 budget passed by the General Assembly increases expenditures by 7.3 percent from this unsustainable base. The Office of State Planning and Budgeting’s June 2002 revenue forecast shows that in fiscal year 2002-03 the State of Colorado will need to reduce General Fund expenditures by $335.5 million given the appropriations level set by the General Assembly. This reduction is necessary in order to maintain the required reserve of two percent of appropriations. This $335.5 million takes into account my line items vetoes and the full amount of the transfer authority allowed by the General Assembly. To date, efforts to reduce general fund expenditures are not sufficient to satisfy the total reductions necessary to comply with the requirement of a balanced budget in Article X, Section 16 of the Colorado Constitution for fiscal year 2002-03. As Governor, I am responsible for restricting the expenditure of state funds if it appears that a revenue shortfall may occur. Colorado Revised Statute § 24-2-102(4) provides: “If, during any fiscal period, there are not sufficient revenues available for expenditure during such period to carry on the functions of the state government and to support its agencies and institutions and such fact is made to appear to the governor, in the exercise of his discretion, by executive order, he may suspend or discontinue, in whole or in part, the functions or services of any department, board, bureau, or agency of the state government…” 2. Mission. I find that there are not sufficient revenues available for expenditure making it necessary to take the cost saving measure of suspending certain functions of state government. Pursuant to C.R.S. § 24-2-102(4), I direct all agencies of state government to assist in meeting the constitutional requirements of a balanced budget, including the suspension of certain contractual terms regarding provider rates due to the fact that funds are not available. 3. Duration. This Executive Order shall remain in force until October 1, 2002 unless modified or terminated by further executive order of the Governor. Pursuant to § 24-2-102(4), I may extend this order by finding that a deficiency of revenues persists. GIVEN under my hand and t h e E x e c u t i v e S e a l o f t h e State of Colorado, this 28th day of June, 2002. B i l l O w e n s G o v e r n o r

full_text: D 020 02 EXECUTIVE ORDER PROCLAMATION CALL FOR THE THIRD EXTRAORDINARY SESSION OF THE SIXTY-THIRD GENERAL ASSEMBLY Pursuant to the authority vested in the Office of the Governor of the State of Colorado, and in particular vested in the Governor pursuant to Article IV, Section 9 of the Colorado Constitution, and as provided for in Article V, Section 7, I, Bill Owens, Governor of the State of Colorado, hereby issue this Executive Order convening the Sixty-Third General Assembly to meet in extraordinary session. 1. Background and Need A. Capital Punishment Statute Colorado’s three-judge panel death sentencing system was established in 1995 after the United States Supreme Court held that a similar system did not violate the United States Constitution in the case of Walton v. Arizona. On July 1, 1995, the State of Colorado implemented Colorado Revised Statute § 16-11-103, which states : “[u]pon conviction of guilt of a defendant of a class 1 felony, a panel of three judges, as soon as practicable, shall conduct a separate sentencing hearing to determine whether the defendant should be sentenced to death or life imprisonment…” In particular, Colorado Revised Statute § 16-11-103(2)(a)(I) requires that the panel must unanimously determine “[w]hether at least one aggravating factor has been proved…” in order to impose the death penalty. Since July 1, 1995, three convicted defendants have been sentenced to death by a three-judge panel. Colorado’s three-judge panel has been a fair and effective system for determining whether the death penalty is appropriate in each case and the death sentence applied in the three cases was the correct decision. The United States Supreme Court recently issued an opinion in the case of Ring v. Arizona that overrules the 1990 case of Walton v. Arizona. The Court has ruled that a jury and not a judge must consider and find the presence of aggravating factors that qualify the defendant for the death penalty. This holding places Colorado’s current death penalty sentencing system in question for future homicides where the death penalty is sought. Immediate measures must be taken to ensure that Colorado has a legally defensible sentencing structure in place for future death sentencing determinations. Due to the import of the Ring v. Arizona decision, an extraordinary occasion has arisen that necessitates that I convene a special session to address the issue of ensuring that Colorado has a Constitutional death penalty statute. B. Wildfire and Drought Colorado is experiencing the most active and destructive wildfire season in state history. Over 350,000 acres have burned throughout the state, with the vast majority of the fire season still ahead of us. Severe drought conditions continue, making the fire danger ever more serious. Wildfires will continue to be a serious long-term threat to our state. State laws must be drafted and adapted to help Colorado meet the risk of wildfires. Human activities have been the most significant cause of wildfires in 2002. In response, on June 10, 2002, I ordered a statewide ban on open burning as well as the sale and use of fireworks. Current state laws deterring and punishing human activities responsible for disasters are insufficient. The wildfire situation indicates the possible need to update and clarify Colorado’s emergency response laws and related criminal statutes. In particular, wildfires constantly pose a significant threat to our citizens’ lives and property and effective laws must be enacted to meet this danger. Colorado’s drought has also reached historic proportions. Many river basins are currently below 10 percent of their normal water capacity and snow pack levels are currently at less than 2 percent of normal level. Concerning the implementation of a capital punishment sentencing structure that comports with the recent decisions of the United States Supreme Court. B. full_text: D 021 02 E X E C U T I V E O R D E R Concerning the Statewide Disaster Emergency Due to Wildfires and the Open Burning Ban and Amending Executive Orders D 014 02, D 015 02 and D 016 02 Pursuant to the authority vested in the Office of the Governor of the State of Colorado, and in particular Article IV, Section 5 of the Colorado Constitution, and Sections 24-32-2100 et seq., and 23-30-308 of the Colorado Revised Statutes, I, Bill Owens, Governor of the State of Colorado, hereby issue this Executive Order declaring that a state of disaster emergency continues to exist due to the imminent threat of wildfires and order the extension of the statewide open burning ban. 1. Background & Need. On June 10, 2002, I issued Executive Order D 014 02 declaring a disaster emergency due to the occurrence of wildfires and the imminent threat of future wildfires. full_text: D 024 02 EXECUTIVE ORDER EXTENSION OF ORDER DIRECTING AGENCIES OF STATE GOVERNMENT TO ASSIST IN MEETING THE CONSTITUTIONAL REQUIREMENTS OF A BALANCED BUDGET Pursuant to the authority vested in the Office of the Governor of the State of Colorado, and in particular Colorado Revised Statute § 24-2-102(4), I, Bill Owens, Governor of the State of Colorado, hereby issue this Executive Order directing agencies of state government to assist in meeting the constitutional requirements of a balanced budget, including the suspension of certain provider rates. This order extends Executive Order D 018 02 as permitted by Colorado Revised Statute § 24-2-102(4). 1. Background and Purpose. The State of Colorado is facing a revenue shortfall, as are most states in the nation. In fiscal year 2001-02, most General Fund expenditures were preserved through $1.2 billion of one-time revenues. Because these were one-time revenue sources, the General Assembly maintained a revenue base in FY 2002-01 that is not sustainable. Nonetheless, the General Assembly’s fiscal year 2002-03 budget increases expenditures by 7.3 percent. The Office of State Planning and Budgeting’s September 2002 revenue forecast shows that in fiscal year 2002-03 the State of Colorado will need to reduce General Fund expenditures by a total of $550 million to maintain the required reserve of two percent of appropriations. The revenue forecast is considerably lower than the previous forecast of June 2002, primarily due to lower income tax and sales tax forecasts. Since June 2002, I have taken action to reduce expenditures by $220 million. The state now must find a way to reduce spending by another $330 million in order to comply with the requirement of a balanced budget in Article X, Section 16 of the Colorado Constitution for fiscal year 2002-03. As Governor, I am responsible for restricting the expenditure of state funds if it appears that a revenue shortfall may occur. Colorado Revised Statute § 24-2-102(4) provides: “If, during any fiscal period, there are not sufficient revenues available for expenditure during such period to carry on the functions of the state government and to support its agencies and institutions and such fact is made to appear to the governor, in the exercise of his discretion, by executive order, he may suspend or discontinue, in whole or in part, the functions or services of any department, board, bureau, or agency of the state government…” 2. Mission. I find that the deficiency of revenues addressed in Executive Order D 018 02 still persists and is growing. Without sufficient revenues available for expenditure, it is necessary to take the cost saving measure of suspending certain functions of state government. Pursuant to C.R.S. § 24-2-102(4), I direct all agencies of state government to continue to assist in meeting the constitutional requirements of a balanced budget. I authorize the suspension or discontinuation, in whole or in part, of certain functions or services of any state department, board, bureau or agency of the state government as determined necessary by the executive director of the affected principal department to comply with Article X, Section 16 of the State Constitution for fiscal year 2002-2003. This order includes the suspension of certain contractual terms regarding provider rates due to the fact that funds are not available. 3. Duration. This Executive Order shall remain in force until January 1, 2003, unless modified or terminated by further Executive Order of the Governor. Pursuant to § 24-2-102(4), I may extend this order by finding that a deficiency of revenues persists. GIVEN under my hand and the Executive Seal of the State of Colorado, this 27th day of September, 2002. B i l l O w e n s G o v e r n o r

full_text: D 025 02 EXECUTIVE ORDER Concerning the Threat of Flooding in Areas Affected by Recent Wildfires Pursuant to the authority vested in the Of fice of the Governor of the State of Colorado, and in particular Section 24-32-2101 et seq. of the Colorado Revised Statutes, I, Bill Owens, Governor of the State of Colorado, hereby issue this Executive Order declaring a disaster emergency due to the imminent threat of flood in areas affected by wildfires. 1. Background and Need. Over the past 5 months, Colorado has experienced the most destructive wildfire season in state history. To date, 2,031 wildfires have burned a total of 501,686 acres throughout the state. While the risk of additional wildfires remains, we must begin the process of restoring areas of this state destroyed during the 2002 fire season. The restoration of soils in watershed areas must be a priority in this recovery effort. The 2002 fires have left many hillsides completely barren. This situation creates a serious risk of flooding, contamination of water sources, and accelerated erosion. For example, in 1996 a wildfire burned 12,000 acres near Buffalo Creek. In the months following the fire, numerous flash floods ensued, culminating in a major flood that claimed two lives, caused extensive damage and left many residents without water for a month. Given the vast acreage consumed by the 2002 wildfires, the state faces a serious risk of floods in the months and years ahead. Immediate measures must be taken to respond to this threat. The United States Department of Agriculture recently released $13 million to the Natural Resource Conservation Service (NRCS) to restore burned watersheds in Colorado. However, access to these funds requires a 25 percent match from non- federal sources. The match can be achieved with cash funding or in kind contributions. One purpose of the Disaster Emergency Act is to “[p]rovide a setting conducive to the rapid and orderly start of restoration and rehabilitation of persons and property affected by disasters;” Colorado Revised Statutes § 24-32-2102. The Act defines disasters as “the occurrence or imminent threat of widespread or severe damage, injury, or loss of life or property resulting from any natural cause or cause of human origin, including but not limited to...flood…” C.R.S. § 24-32-2103(1.5). The risk of flood in areas affected by the 2002 wildfires poses an imminent threat to the life and property of Colorado citizens. Federal funds are needed to begin soil restoration projects in these high-risk areas. Therefore, I authorize up to $2 million from the Disaster Emergency Fund to be used as matching funds for fire restoration projects and order state agencies to participate in these efforts. 2. Mission and Scope. The threat of flooding in areas burned by wildfires poses an imminent threat to the life and property of people living in these areas. This threat constitutes a disaster emergency for the purposes of C.R.S. § 24-32-2103. In accordance with this threat, I hereby authorize the use of up to $2 million of disaster emergency funds. These funds may be used as a 25 percent match to receive federal assistance with the fire restoration efforts. I order appropriate state agencies to participate in soil restoration projects that qualify as in kind contributions for purposes of this project. These services will reduce the cash funded portion of the NRCS match. 3. Duration. This Executive Order shall expire thirty (30) days from the date of its execution unless extended by Executive Order. GIVEN under my hand and the Executive Seal of the State of Colorado, this 30th day of September, 2002. Bill Owens Governor

full_text: D 026 02 EXECUTIVE ORDER Requiring the Attorney General To Prosecute All Criminal Actions and Proceedings in the Seventh Judicial District Pursuant to the authority vested in the Of fice of the Governor of the State of Colorado, and in particular Article IV, Section 2 of the Colorado Constitution and Section 24-31-101 of the Colorado Revised Statutes, I, Bill Owens, Governor of the State of Colorado require the Attorney General to prosecute all actions and proceedings in the Seventh Judicial District in which the state is a party. 1. Background and Need. Wyatt Angelo has resigned from the elected position of district attorney in the Seventh Judicial District, effective midnight October 6, 2002. Under Colorado Revised Statute § 20-1-201(1)(a) the deputy district attorneys “hold their offices during the pleasure of such district attorney.” It is necessary to assure the continuation of the functions of the office of the district attorney in the Seventh Judicial District upon the resignation of Wyatt Angelo. Colorado Revised Statute § 24-31-101 provides that the Attorney General “shall appear for the state and prosecute and defend all actions and proceedings, civil and criminal, in which the state is a party or is interested when required to do so by the governor…” Under this provi sion, the Attorney General must prosecute criminal matters when required to do so by the Governor. An assistant attorney general that prosecutes a case under the authority of C.R.S. § 24- 31-101 is exercising the district attorney’s powers: "[W]hen the governor or the general assembly requires the attorney general to prosecute a criminal case in which the state is a party, he becomes to all intents and purposes the district attorney, and may in his own name and official capacity exercise all the powers of such officer, for he is then, and in that case, the public prosecutor. Being authorized and empowered to appear and prosecute, he can do each and everything essential to prosecute in accordance with the law of the land . . . ." People v. Gibson, 53 Colo. 231 (1912); People ex rel. Witcher v. District Court, 190 Colo. 483 (1976). A special assistant attorney general is empowered to prosecute criminal matters in the Seventh Judicial District with the same authority as a district attorney. As provided in C.R.S. § 24-31-101(f)(3), the Attorney General may appoint the existing deputy district attorneys in the Seventh Judicial District as special assistant attorneys general: “The attorney general may appoint such deputies and assistants as are necessary for the efficient operations of his office…” By the authority cited above, I am requiring the Attorney General to prosecute criminal matters in which the state is a party in the Seventh Judicial District, effective 12:01 a.m. on October 7, 2002. The Attorney General has agreed that the most effective means of carrying out these duties is to appoint the assistant district attorney, the chief deputy district attorney and the deputy district attorneys in the Seventh Judicial District as special assistant attorneys general. All other appointees of the district attorney shall retain their existing authority. 2. Mission and Scope. Pursuant to C.R.S. § 24-31-101(1)(a), I hereby require the Attorney General to appear for the state and prosecute all criminal actions and proceedings in which the state is a party in the Seventh Judicial District. 3. Duration. This Executive Order shall remain in force until modified or terminated by further executive order of the Governor or until I appoint a district attorney pursuant to Article VI, Section 20(4) of the Colorado Constitution for the Seventh Judicial District. GIVEN under my hand and the Executive Seal of the State of Colorado, this 6 th day of October, 2002. Bill Owens Governor

full_text: D 001 03 E X E C U T I V E O R D E R RELOCATING OFFICE FOR CERTIFICATION FOR MINORITY BUSINESSES Pursuant to the authority vested in the Office of the Governor of the State of Colorado, I, Bill Owens, Governor of the State of Colorado, hereby issue this Executive Order declaring that the State Office of Certification shall be removed from the Colorado Department of Regulatory Agencies and shall be located and administered under the Center for Equal Opportunity of the Colorado Department of Transportation. 1. Background and Need Executive Order D 0055 87 moved the Office of Certification for minority businesses (also known as Disadvantaged Business Enterprises, or “DBEs”) from the Colorado Department of Transportation (“CDOT”) to the Colorado Department of Regulatory Agencies (“DORA”). Still, CDOT retained the ultimate responsibility for the DBE certification process and provided a majority of the Office’s funding. Currently, CDOT funds seventy percent of the Certification Office budget. The remainder of the Office’s funding comes from contracts with other governmental entities. It will be more efficient to conduct the DBE certification process within CDOT. The Center for Equal Opportunity manages the DBE program within CDOT and will have direct supervision over the certification process. This will increase performance and accountability in the DBE certification process by facilitating communication and streamlining administrative matters. The departments estimate that the State would save approximately $50,000 in the first year by moving the DBE certification process back to CDOT, with additional cost savings expected in future years. Budget savings should be realized wherever possible, especially during the current budget shortfall. Furthermore, this is generally considered the most efficient location for this state program; a recent DORA study found that almost ninety percent of other states manage their DBE certification program within the state’s department of transportation. 2. Declaration Accordingly, I hereby issue this executive order declaring that the State Office of Certification, along with its employees and resources, as determined by the Executive Director of DORA, shall be transferred from DORA to CDOT. The Office of Certification will be established within the Center for Equal Opportunity under CDOT. Within the constraints of applicable federal laws and regulations, the Executive Director 2 of CDOT shall have the authority to establish the functions and personnel of the Office of Certification at CDOT in the most effective and efficient manner, including merging the functions into the Center and abolishing the Office in name. 3. Past Executive Orders Superceded and Replaced This Executive Order shall repeal and replace all previous executive order provisions pertaining to the relocation of the Office of Certification, and specifically Paragraph 4 of Executive Order D 0055 87. GIVEN under my hand and the Executive Seal of the State of Colorado, this 8th day of January, 2003. Bill Owens Governor

full_text: D 002 03 EXECUTIVE ORDER Directing State Agencies To Coordinate Efforts for the Eradication of Tamarisk on State Lands Pursuant to the authority vested in the Office of the Governor of the State of Colorado, I, Bill Owens, Governor of the State of Colorado, hereby issue this Executive Order directing the Colorado Department of Natural Resources, in consultation and cooperation with other appropriate state and federal agencies, to coordinate efforts to eradicate the tamarisk plant on public lands. 1. Background and Purpose The State of Colorado, like the rest of the Western United States, faces the immense challenge of dealing with noxious weeds that cause harm to the ecosystem. The most destructive non-native invasive species in Colorado is the tamarisk plant, also known as saltcedar. Tamarisk is rapidly spreading throughout Colorado and the surrounding region. Efforts to control this aggressive plant species have been unsuccessful. It is now estimated that the plant has overcome native species on 1.5 million acres throughout the region and it is has become apparent that the plant is causing serious ecological and environmental problems within the State of Colorado. The tamarisk plant consumes an enormous amount of water. A single tamarisk tree can transpire up to 300 gallons of water per day. As a comparison, an average acre of native cottonwood trees uses 845,000 gallons of water per year, while an acre of tamarisk uses 1.3 million gallons of water per year. An accumulation of tamarisk plants close to a watershed can effectively limit or dry up an entire water source. The disproportionate consumption of water by a non-native invasive species is cause for serious concern for Colorado as it continues to endure one of the worst droughts in state history. In addition, tamarisk species are inedible to most animals. As a result, wildlife over browse the surviving native plant species, further speeding the tamarisk invasion process. Finally, tamarisk trees produce extremely flammable leaf litter which promotes the incidence of wildfire. Given the devastating effect of this non-native species, I am directing state agencies to take appropriate measures to eradicate tamarisk on public lands. 2. Mission I hereby direct the Department of Natural Resources, the Department of Agriculture and any other state agency that may prove helpful with this project, to take measures necessary to eradicate tamarisk on public lands within ten years of this Executive Order. State agencies participating in this project shall designate a point of contact to coordinate tamarisk assessment and removal efforts, and to identify necessary funding sources. The Department of Natural Resources shall coordinate these efforts and, within one year of the effective date of this order, shall submit a report to the Governor’s Office outlining a viable plan to achieve the eradication of tamarisk in Colorado within ten years. 3. Duration This Executive Order shall remain in effect until modified or rescinded by Executive Order. GIVEN under my hand and the Executive Seal of the State of Colorado, this 8th day of January, 2003. Bill Owens Governor

full_text: D 003 03 EXECUTIVE ORDER Concerning the Continuing Threat of Flooding in Areas Affected by the 2002 Wildfires Pursuant to the authority vested in the Of fice of the Governor of the State of Colorado, and in particular Section 24-32-2101 et seq. of the Colorado Revised Statutes, I, Bill Owens, Governor of the State of Colorado, hereby issue this Executive Order declaring a disaster emergency due to the imminent threat of flood in areas affected by wildfires. 1. Background and Need. In 2002, 2,031 wildfires burned a total of 501,686 acres throughout the State of Colorado. As a result of these fires, many hillsides throughout the state are completely barren. This situation creates a serious risk of flooding, contamination of water sources, and accelerated erosion. For example, in 1996 a wildfire burned 12,000 acres near Buffalo Creek. In the months following the fire, numerous flash floods ensued, culminating in a major flood that claimed two lives, caused extensive damage and left many residents without water for a month. One purpose of the Disaster Emergency Act is to “[p]rovide a setting conducive to the rapid and orderly start of restoration and rehabilitation of persons and property affected by disasters;” Colorado Revised Statutes § 24-32-2102. The Act defines disasters as “the occurrence or imminent threat of widespread or severe damage, injury, or loss of life or property resulting from any natural cause or cause of human origin, including but not limited to...flood…” C.R.S. § 24-32-2103(1.5). The United States Department of Agriculture has released $13 million to the Natural Resource Conservation Service (NRCS) to restore burned watersheds in Colorado. However, access to these funds requires a 25 percent match from non-federal sources. The match can be achieved with cash funding or in kind contributions. On September 30, 2002, I issued Executive Order D 025 02, declaring that the 2002 wildfires have created a threat of flooding that constitutes a disaster emergency for the purposes of Colorado Revised Statute Section 24-32-2101 et seq. Executive Order D 025 02 authorized up to $2 million from the Disaster Emergency Fund to be used as matching funds for fire restoration projects. The risk of flood in areas affected by the 2002 wildfires continues to pose an imminent threat to the life and property of Colorado citizens. 2. Mission and Scope. The threat of flooding in areas burned by wildfires poses an imminent threat to the life and property of people living in these areas. This threat constitutes a disaster emergency for the purposes of C.R.S. § 24-32-2103. In accordance with this threat, I hereby authorize the continued use of Disaster Funds made available in Executive Order D 025 02. These funds may be used as a 25 percent match to receive federal assistance with the fire restoration efforts and shall remain available for that purpose until June 8, 2003. This order does not increase the amount of available funds. I order appropriate state agencies to continue to participate in soil restoration projects that qualify as in kind contributions for purposes of this project. These services will reduce the cash funded portion of the NRCS match. 3. Duration. This Executive Order shall expire thirty (30) days from the date of its execution unless extended by Executive Order. GIVEN under my hand and the Executive Seal of the State of Colorado, this 8th day of January, 2003. Bill Owens Governor

full_text: D 004 03 E X E C U T I V E O R D E R PROCLAMATION CONCERNING THE NAME OF THE GOVERNOR’S RESIDENCE Pursuant to the authority vested in the Office of the Governor of the State of Colorado, I, Bill Owens, Governor of the State of Colorado, hereby issue this Executive Order naming the executive mansion. 1. Background and Need In 1924, Claude K. Boettcher purchased what is now the executive mansion and resided there with his family. The Boettchers acquired remarkable furnishings and artwork from all parts of the world, many of which remain part of the mansion collection. The Boettchers remodeled and expanded the mansion, including enclosing the former porch to create the Palm Room with its floor-to-ceiling windows bearing the Boettcher family initials. The remodeled desk, created by the most celebrated of Louis XIV furniture makers and designers, is said to be one of only two in existence. When the Boettchers passed away, they left the mansion to a private family foundation to be given to the State of Colorado for use as a governors' residence. Colorado’s governors have occupied the residence since 1959. The State of Colorado is grateful for the generous gift from the Boettcher Foundation, and for the Foundation’s continued support in maintaining the residence as a historic Colorado landmark. The mansion and its effects are a testament to the Boettcher family’s substantial involvement in establishing the mansion as the Governor’s residence, and the name given to the mansion should also reflect this family’s benevolent contribution to our State. 2 2. Declaration Accordingly, I hereby issue this executive order declaring that the executive mansion at 400 East 8th Avenue in Denver shall hereafter be named the “Governor’s Residence at the Boettcher Mansion.” GIVEN under my hand and the Executive Seal of the State of Colorado, this twenty-second day of January, 2003. full_text: D 005 03 EXECUTIVE ORDER Concerning State Employee Travel Pursuant to the authority vested in the Office of the Governor of the State of Colorado, I, Bill Owens, Governor of the State of Colorado, hereby issue this Executive Order concerning state employee travel. 1. Background and Purpose A recent performance audit of the Statewide Travel Management Program revealed that state employees traveling on official business have cost the taxpayers of the State of Colorado 4.3 million dollars more than necessary by failing to utilize several common sense cost saving strategies. For example, according to the report, state travelers spent $16,700 on unnecessary car rental insurance. State travelers who irresponsibly use their state issued travel cards for personal expenditures on which they default cost the State of Colorado $42,000 a year in volume savings and state employees spent $1.1 million unnecessarily on late purchases of airline tickets. Employees who failed to secure less expensive Internet airfare rates lost significant savings opportunities for the taxpayers of our state. The state auditor’s report confirms that the State of Colorado lacks an adequate system to monitor employee travel and the expenses generated through this travel. While a Colorado Statewide Travel Management Program has been in place since 1994, the state auditor makes a compelling case for reform of this system. That is why I support and plan to sign Senate Bill 243 if it is adopted by the General Assembly to abolish this program effective July 1, 2004. In light of the need to reform Colorado’s state employee travel policies, I am directing all executive departments of state government to adopt new procedures to take advantage of the savings available to the State of Colorado through increased vigilance of our official business travel activities. By this Executive Order I am encouraging Institutions of Higher Education to adopt consistent procedures to accomplish these travel reforms. It is my intention that all travel management reforms including their implementation and enforcement will be accomplished using existing state resources. 2. Directive To better manage the State of Colorado’s necessary employee travel expenses I direct the following: A. Procedures for approved state travel Each executive director of a principal department of state government or his or her designee shall require pre-approval in writing of all out-of-state travel performed by their state employees. Each executive director of a principal department of state government shall designate an individual to be responsible for overseeing compliance and enforcement of travel rules and policies. The Department of Personnel and Administration shall develop rules requiring submission of receipts for reimbursement for per diem allowances unless the executive director’s travel compliance designee approves the purchases in writing. I direct the Department of Personnel and Administration to educate director’s travel compliance designees, department controllers, and department purchasing agents concerning proper oversight, compliance and enforcement actions pursuant to the rules required to be developed by this Executive Order. The Department of Personnel and Administration shall adopt rules and procedures to expressly permit the purchase of Internet airfares if the Internet fare will achieve a cost savings compared to purchase through an approved state travel agent. B. Procedures for a State of Colorado travel card Effective May 1, 2003, the State of Colorado will utilize a new state travel credit card to facilitate transactions regarding necessary and approved state employee travel. I direct the Department of Personnel and Administration to develop appropriate rules and regulations to require that this state travel card be used for both in-state and out-of-state travel purposes. It is my intent through this directive to enable employees to use their individual state travel card or the applicable department, agency or institution state travel card for official business travel purposes. Purchases with a state travel card are currently restricted to expenses incurred for the benefit of the state and completed using the most economical means available which will satisfactorily accomplish the state’s business. Nevertheless, some purchases are made that do not legitimately relate to official state business. Therefore, I direct the Department of Personnel and Administration to develop appropriate rules and regulations to require state employees who make purchases in violation of the state benefit rule personally responsible for payment of those unauthorized purchases. Similarly, the Department of Personnel and Administration shall seek to amend the state personnel rules if necessary to subject a state employee who fails to pay his or her state issued travel card bill to disciplinary action including termination from employment with the state at the discretion of the employee’s hiring authority. C. Rental car use I request that the Department of Personnel and Administration use best efforts to negotiate a provision in the July 2003 car rental contract that includes penalties if car rental companies awarded state contracts sell unnecessary insurance to state employees. I direct the Department of Personnel and Administration to develop rules and regulations preventing state employees who accept unnecessary automobile rental insurance from receiving reimbursement for the purchase of this insurance. D. Travel to Washington D.C. The State of Colorado spends an estimated 7.5 million dollars in travel to the Washington, D.C. area. Some of this travel is unnecessary or duplicative. Accordingly, I direct all principal departments of state government to submit travel plans to the Office of the Governor’s travel designee in advance of travel to Washington, D.C. Travel plans required by this subsection shall include, the purpose of the trip, length of stay, the cost of the trip, intended source of payment for the trip, and a schedule of all appointments with any member of Congress or his or her staff or federal government department or agency personnel. E. Institutions of Higher Education I instruct the executive director of the Colorado Commission on Higher Education to develop a proposed travel policy consistent with this Executive Order for consideration by the Colorado Commission on Higher Education. The executive director shall work with the Commission to achieve adoption of a travel policy pursuant to the Commission’s authority to establish system-wide policies concerning administrative costs. In the interim, I encourage the Presidents of state-supported institutions of higher education to adopt their own travel policies to coordinate with this Executive Order, including requiring written pre-approval for all out-of- state travel, procedures governing reimbursement accountability and procedures allowing maximum cost savings. F. International Travel This Executive Order recognizes that international travel authorization is required pursuant to State of Colorado Fiscal Rule 5-1 .03. This rule provides: “Prior written or electronic authorization by the chief executive officer, or a delegate, of a state agency and the governor, or a delegate, shall be required for all international travel, except for the Department of Higher Education. Prior written authorization by the executive director of the Colorado Commission on Higher education shall be required for all international travel by employees within the Department of Higher Education. The executive director of the Colorado Commission on Higher Education, with approval of the State Controller, may delegate the authority to approve international travel to the chief executive officer, or a delegate, of a specific higher education institution.” 3. Implementation All departmental changes necessary to implement the reforms contained in this Executive Order shall be made within existing budgetary appropriations. Departments shall not seek additional resources from the legislature to comply with the provisions of this Executive Order. 4. Duration This Executive Order shall remain in force until modified or terminated by further executive order of the Governor. GIVEN under my hand and t h e E x e c u t i v e S e a l o f t h e State of Colorado, this 17th day of March, 2003. B i l l O w e n s G o v e r n o r

full_text: D 007 03 EXECUTIVE ORDER EXTENSION OF ORDER DIRECTING AGENCIES OF STATE GOVERNMENT TO ASSIST IN MEETING THE CONSTITUTIONAL REQUIREMENTS OF A BALANCED BUDGET Pursuant to the authority vested in the Office of the Governor of the State of Colorado, and in particular Colorado Revised Statute § 24-2-102(4), I, Bill Owens, Governor of the State of Colorado, hereby issue this Executive Order directing agencies of state government to assist in meeting the constitutional requirements of a balanced budget, including the suspension of certain provider rates. This order extends Executive Order D 031 02 as permitted by Colorado Revised Statute § 24-2-102(4). 1. Background and Purpose. The State of Colorado is facing a revenue shortfall, as are most states in the nation. In fiscal year 2001-02, most General Fund expenditures were preserved through $1.1 billion of one-time revenues. Because these were one-time revenue sources, the General Assembly maintained a revenue base in FY 2001-02 that is not sustainable. Nonetheless, the General Assembly’s fiscal year 2002-03 budget increased expenditures by 7.3 percent. In fiscal year 2002-03 the State of Colorado will need to reduce General Fund expenditures by a total of $784 million to maintain the required reserve of two percent of appropriations. The revenue forecast is lower than the previous forecast of December 2002, primarily due to lower income tax and individual and corporate forecasts. Thus far, we have taken action to address $809 million of this year’s budget shortfall. Nonetheless, revenue shortfalls are expected to continue and additional action may be necessary in order to comply with the requirement of a balanced budget in Article X, Section 16 of the Colorado Constitution for fiscal year 2002-03. As Governor, I am responsible for restricting the expenditure of state funds if it appears that a revenue shortfall may occur. Colorado Revised Statute § 24-2-102(4) provides: “If, during any fiscal period, there are not sufficient revenues available for expenditure during such period to carry on the functions of the state government and to support its agencies and institutions and such fact is made to appear to the governor, in the exercise of his discretion, by executive order, he may suspend or discontinue, in whole or in part, the functions or services of any department, board, bureau, or agency of the state government…” 2. Mission. I find that the deficiency of revenues addressed in Executive Order D 031 02 persists. Without sufficient revenues available for appropriated expenditures, it is necessary to take the cost saving measure of suspending certain functions of state government. Pursuant to C.R.S. § 24-2-102(4), I direct all agencies of state government to continue to assist in meeting the constitutional requirements of a balanced budget. I authorize the suspension or discontinuation, in whole or in part, of certain functions or services of any state department, board, bureau or agency of the state government as determined necessary by the executive director of the affected principal department to comply with Article X, Section 16 of the State Constitution for fiscal year 2002-2003. This order includes the suspension of certain contractual terms regarding provider rates due to the fact that funds are not available. 3. Duration. This Executive Order shall remain in force until July 1, 2003, unless modified or terminated by further Executive Order of the Governor. Pursuant to § 24-2-102(4), I may extend this order by finding that a deficiency of revenues persists. GIVEN under my hand and the Executive Seal of the State of Colorado, this 25th day of March, 2003. B i l l O w e n s G o v e r n o r

full_text: D 006 03 EXECUTIVE ORDER Declaring a Disaster Emergency Due to a Severe Winter Storm Pursuant to the authority vested in the Governor of the State of Colorado and, in particular, pursuant to relevant portions of the Colorado Disaster Emergency Act, §§ 24-32-2100 et seq., C.R.S. I, Bill Owens, Governor of the State of Colorado, hereby issue this Executive Order declaring a state of disaster emergency due to a severe winter storm. 1. Background and Need Between March 17, 2003 and March 20, 2003, a powerful blizzard covered most of Colorado. This was one of largest snowstorms in Colorado’s history. The Denver metro area received over two and one half feet of snow while many suburbs received much more. Numerous locations throughout the state received over six feet of snow. As a result of the heavy snowfall, roads and highways became increasingly dangerous for motorists. Many travelers were unable to reach their destinations and local emergency personnel were overwhelmed by the task of rescuing stranded motorists. In several situations, emergency vehicles were not capable of navigating the dangerous roads to reach the vehicles. With increasing snowfall and dropping temperatures this became a dangerous situation for the trapped motorists. In addition, this situation restricted emergency vehicles from responding to calls and reaching individuals in need of medical attention. As Governor, I am responsible for meeting the dangers to the state and people presented by disasters. The Colorado Disaster Emergency Act (hereinafter the “Act”), defines a disaster as “the occurrence or imminent threat of widespread or severe damages, injury or loss of life or property resulting from any natural cause or cause of human origin, including but not limited to…storm.” C.R.S. § 24-32-2103(1.5). As detailed above, this snowstorm posed an imminent danger to human life and, therefore, constituted a disaster for the purposes of the Act. In response to this disaster, I ordered certain elements of the Colorado National Guard to active duty to assist with emergency response as a result of the snowstorm. Specifically, I authorized the activation of National Guard troops and the use of emergency equipment. The Colorado Office of Emergency Management estimates that 39 soldiers were called to active duty and 5 Snow Utility Vehicles and 13 Humvees were utilized in the assignment. These crews coordinated with local authorities to rescue stranded motorists, guide emergency vehicles to urgent situations and deliver individuals in need of emergency care to hospitals. 2. Mission and Scope A. I hereby declare that this snowstorm constituted a disaster for purposes of C.R.S. §24- 32-2103, and acknowledge my earlier verbal order declaring a statewide disaster emergency, activating the State Emergency Operations Plan and activating certain elements of the Colorado National Guard. B. Pursuant to C.R.S. § 24-32-2106, I order the encumbrance of up to $50,000 from the State Disaster Emergency Fund to pay for Colorado National Guard personnel and equipment used to assist in this disaster emergency response effort. These funds shall remain available for this purpose for six months from the date of this Executive Order. C. The Director of the Colorado Office of Emergency Management is hereby authorized and directed to coordinate application to the federal government for any funds for public assistance disaster relief and for other funding related to the disaster emergency. D. All verbal orders that I issued in regards to this disaster emergency, including my disaster emergency declaration on March 19, 2003, is hereby memorialized by this Executive Order and shall have the full force and effect of law as if they were contained within this Executive Order. 3. Duration This Executive Order shall expire thirty days from its date of signature unless extended by Executive Order. Given under my hand and the Executive Seal of the State of Colorado this 26th day of March, 2003. Bill Owens Governor

full_text: D 010 03 EXECUTIVE ORDER Authorizing the Hiring of Outside Counsel Pursuant to the authority vested in th e Office of the Governor of the State of Colorado, and in particular Article IV, Section 2 of the Colorado Constitution, and Section 24-31-101(1)(e) of the Colorado Revised Statutes I, Bill Owens, Governor of the State of Colorado, hereby issue this Executive Order authorizing the Governor, the Secretary of State and any other interested state agency to hire outside counsel. 1. Background and Need On May 5, 2003, Attorney General Ken Salazar sent a letter to the leaders of the Colorado General Assembly stating that the Office of the Attorney General will not provide legal services to any state agency on matters related to Senate Bill 03- 352. “Because I believe the bill undermines the constitutional redistricting framework, I will (1) refuse to defend the State defendants in that action and (2) on behalf of the people of Colorado, I will support the claim that SB 352 is unconstitutional.” On May 9, 2003, plaintiffs Maryanne Keller and Pauline York brought an action in Denver District Court naming Secretary of State Donetta Davidson and the General Assembly as defendants. In their complaint, plaintiffs challenge among other things the constitutionality of Senate Bill 352. On May 16, 2003, the Keller plaintiffs added Governor Bill Owens as a named defendant in their lawsuit. On May 14, 2003, the Attorney General filed a petition for original jurisdiction with the Colorado Supreme Court seeking to enjoin the Secretary of State from enforcing Senate Bill 352. On May 15, 2003, the Colorado Supreme Court issued an Order and Rule to Show Cause that required the Secretary of State to submit an answer to the Court as to why the Attorney General’s petition should not be granted. The Court’s order also invited the Governor and “other interested persons” to file briefs with the Court. Colorado Revised Statutes §24-31-101(1)(e) states, “Whenever the attorney general is unable or has failed or refused to provide legal services to an agency of state government, as determined by the governor if the agency is in the executive branch or by the chief justice if the agency is in the judicial branch, such agency may employ counsel of its own choosing to provide such legal services. Any expense incurred by reason of the employment of counsel pursuant to this paragraph (e) shall be a lawful charge against appropriations for this purpose made by the general assembly to the department of law.” The Attorney General has refused to provide legal services to any state agency on issues pertaining to this matter. This Executive Order authorizes the Governor, the Secretary of State and any other interested state agency to hire outside counsel to defend its interests in this matter. 2. Directive Based on the facts recited above, I find that the requirements of C.R.S. § 24-31- 101(1)(e) are met. I authorize the Office of the Governor, the Secretary of State and any other interested state agency under the executive branch to employ counsel of its own choosing to provide legal services related to the above referenced matter. All expenses occurred thereof shall be charged in accordance with C.R.S. §24-31-101(e) and may be billed back to the May 9, 2003 filing date for Keller v. Davidson et al. GIVEN under my hand and the Executive Seal of the State of Colorado, this 21st day of May, 2003. Bill Owens Governor
